undesired weight gain, best to evaluate eating habits and adjust diet.

Recommend at least 30 minutes of exercise each day as opposed to taking phentermine.
reply:
Glad to hear your surgery went well! You're now clear to resume all of your regular home medications, so phentermine is safe to take from that standpoint.

That said, I'd encourage you to think carefully before restarting it. Rather than relying on medication, I'd recommend taking a closer look at your eating habits and making some adjustments there — that approach tends to have much better long-term results for weight management. I'd also suggest aiming for at least 30 minutes of exercise each day, which can make a real difference over time.

The changes in appetite you're noticing after surgery are understandable, but diet and movement will serve you better in the long run than phentermine will.

patientMessage: About 5 weeks ago I walked into a large plate glass door and hit my brow bone. Came out immediately into a large lump and had a black eye for over a week. Although swelling has gone down, there is still a lump on the eyebrow bone which feels like solid bone.

The lump you're feeling is a haematoma — a collection that formed after the impact. It's hardened over time, which is why it now feels like solid bone. This is a normal part of the healing process, and it will gradually reduce in size on its own.

In the meantime, you can take a painkiller or anti-inflammatory if it's bothering you.

Get back in touch if you have any concerns as things progress.

patientMessage: Hi, I suffer from a red patch over my nose on the left side and right, worse more so on the left. I have been told by my previous doctor that it is eczema and have tried non-prescribed and prescribed creams and nothing seems to clear it up. I have also tried to change eating and drinking habits but no change. It also flares up more so every now and again with no reason as to why. Is there anything I can do? please help
doctorNotes:
keep a possibility of seborrhea dermatitis, can present as red scaly patches on sebaceous gland rich areas like scalp, face, chest etc.
Use a moderately potent topical steroid cream like fluticasone propionate cream twice daily for the initial 2 weeks.
Seborrhea dermatitis often recurs and not advisable to use topical steroids on face for long - therefore after 2 weeks steroids should be replaced with a topical immunomodulator e.g. either pimecrolimus or tacrolimus
reply:
Thank you for reaching out, and I'm sorry to hear how much this has been troubling you — it's clear you've already put a lot of effort into trying to get this sorted, and I want to help.

Looking at what you've described, the pattern of redness across the nose area that flares up from time to time could be consistent with a condition called seborrhoeic dermatitis. This is different from regular eczema — it tends to affect areas of the skin that are rich in oil glands, such as the face, scalp, and chest, and it can cause red, sometimes scaly patches that come and go without any obvious trigger. This may explain why the previous treatments haven't fully worked.

Here's what I'd like you to try:

To start with, I'd like you to use **fluticasone propionate cream**, which is a moderately potent steroid cream, **twice a day for the first two weeks**. This should help calm the inflammation.

Because steroid creams aren't suitable for long-term use on the face, after those two weeks I'd like you to switch to a different type of cream called a **topical immunomodulator** — either **pimecrolimus** or **tacrolimus**. This is better suited for ongoing management of this condition.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis can recur, so please don't be disheartened if it comes back at some point — it's simply the nature of this condition, and we now have a better plan in place to manage it.

Please don't hesitate to get back in touch if you have any questions or if things aren't improving. You're not alone in dealing with this.

patientMessage: Hi, I am Kiran. For the last 3-4 years, I have had a sneezing problem. Once I start sneezing the whole day it goes on some times. Morning sneezes are frequent. Otherwise normally I am perfectly alright, no running nose. I am 25 years old. Weight 60kgs; Height 165 cms. I have consulted a previous doctor once, but he said it might be an allergy problem, so no cure. I just wanted to know what is the cause of this problem and how it can be cured
doctorNotes:
Allergic rhinitis, usually seasonal due to pollen grains, grass, dander or plain dust.
Early morning rhinitis usually due to congestion of the nasal mucosa.
Identify the allergen and try to avoid exposure.
Allopathic treatment consists of decongestants as tablets or as nasal spray
reply:
Hi Kiran,

Your symptoms do point toward allergic rhinitis — essentially, your nose is reacting to something in your environment, such as pollen, grass, animal dander, or dust. The early morning sneezing fits in particular are very typical of this condition, where the nasal lining becomes congested overnight and reacts strongly when you wake up.

The good news is that this can be managed. The first step is trying to identify what you're allergic to so you can reduce your exposure to it as much as possible. On the treatment side, there are medications available — both tablets and nasal sprays — that help relieve the congestion and sneezing.

I'd recommend speaking with your doctor about allergy testing to pinpoint the trigger, and to discuss which treatment option suits you best.

Best wishes,

reply:
Thank you for reaching out and for sharing the images and prescription.

After reviewing everything, your son appears to have a mild case of urticaria — a type of rash that can be triggered by various things such as food, dust, an insect bite, or a viral fever. Given that he had a fever around the same time the rash appeared, the two are likely connected.

Urticaria often behaves exactly the way you've described — flaring up in the evenings and looking clearer in the mornings. The good news is that it's not a cause for alarm. It can persist anywhere from a few weeks up to about 45 days, but it does go away completely on its own.

Please continue with the Zempred (Methylprednisolone) and Levocet (Levocetirizine) as prescribed.

Get back in touch if the rash worsens significantly or if you have any concerns along the way.

patientMessage: Hello doctor, I have been going to a dentist about a tooth that is sore. They started a root canal but then did not finish. I have gone back several times and every time they open up the tooth and insert medicine. My tooth is in agony right now. I am just wondering if this is a standard procedure during a root canal? Should not the dentist remove the nerves so I am not in so much pain? Or is it the standard procedure to fight the infection first and then remove the nerves?
doctorNotes:
The treatment of choice for an infected tooth is a root canal therapy.
Dentist can determine whether nerve is viable or not. If necrosis, they will remove dead tissue. If viable, they will clean out the canals and fill them with a sealer. Then the tooth should be restored with a crown
Should be no further discomfort after procedure
reply:
Your dentist is doing exactly the right thing here. Root canal treatment for an infected tooth typically involves a few steps, and what you're describing sounds like a standard approach.

During the process, your dentist will assess the nerve to determine its condition. If the nerve tissue has died (what we call necrosis), they will remove that dead tissue. If the nerve is still alive, the canals inside the tooth are thoroughly cleaned out and then sealed. Once the root canal is complete, the tooth will need to be restored with a crown to protect it long-term.

The good news is that once the treatment is finished, you should not have any further discomfort from that tooth.

If the pain feels unmanageable in the meantime, it's worth reaching out to your dentist directly so they're aware of how much discomfort you're experiencing.

patientMessage: Hello doctor, Is there a difference in alcoholic and non-alcoholic mouthwash. Which is better at combating bad breath due to smoking than alcoholic? I am in a hygiene school and want to know whether or not to recommend non-alcohol mouthwash for the complaints of bad breath from smoking. I have recommended tongue scraping, alcoholic mouthwash. Anyways, they are not going to stop smoking or drinking. I was looking at a way to have them not dry out the tissues, but stopping the obvious factors do not seem to be an option.
doctorNotes:
Mouthwash w chlorhexidine (0.12%) very effective in controlling halitosis, it is antibacterial to control bad breath.
Also keeps gums healthy and prevents plaque formation.
Alcohol free mouthwashes can cause irritation to the mucosa lining the mouth and may worsen bad breath.
Advise chlorhexidine mouthwash if you smoke. May need to use for ~3 months to see visible results
reply:
Good question, and it's great that you're thinking carefully about what to recommend for your patients.

For people who smoke and are struggling with bad breath, chlorhexidine mouthwash (0.12%) is a strong choice. It's antibacterial, which directly targets the bacteria responsible for halitosis, and it also supports gum health and helps prevent plaque buildup — all useful benefits for smokers.

On the alcohol-free versus alcoholic question: alcohol-free mouthwashes can actually cause irritation to the mucosal lining of the mouth and may end up making bad breath worse, so they're not necessarily the better option here. Chlorhexidine mouthwash would be the recommendation for patients who smoke.

One thing worth setting expectations around — it can take around three months of consistent use before visible results are noticeable, so it's worth letting your patients know upfront so they stick with it.

Hope that helps with your recommendations.

patientMessage: I am a 30 yr old female that has been experiencing an irregular heart beat brought on by possible stress of starting a new position at work. Ever since I atarted it my heart has had random episodes of quick beats to where it feels like two at a time. Its noticeable and I'm wondering what's wrong. No change if anything other than my job.
doctorNotes:
Two beats which you feel in succession may be because of extra beats.
The change in job and early anxiety about fitting into a new place may increase the stress hormones like cortisol.
Both situations are completely benign and just some relaxation techniques would help.
If it's too troublesome, a 24-hour Holter monitor would be the best test to evaluate the same, or an EKG during the episode.
For your age, rule out thyroid as the cause if associated symptoms are present.
will set up a time to discuss these options
reply:
What you're feeling — those rapid beats that seem to come in pairs — could be extra beats, which can sometimes happen with the kind of stress that comes with starting a new job. The adjustment period, the pressure to fit in, all of that can raise stress hormones like cortisol, and that in turn can trigger these sensations. The good news is that both of these things — the extra beats and stress-related changes — are completely harmless.

Some relaxation techniques may go a long way in helping settle things down. That said, if the episodes become more bothersome, there are a couple of tests worth considering: a 24-hour Holter monitor, which records your heart rhythm over a full day, or an EKG taken during one of the episodes. Given your age and these symptoms, it would also be worth checking your thyroid if you notice any other related symptoms alongside the irregular beats.

I'll be in touch to set up a time for us to talk through these options together.

patientMessage: I am a smoker and i have an tooth ache really bad i think infection is involved. i used pain meds and hydrogen peroxide to help with pain will see my dentist asap. i am a smoker it does not seem to bother me just trying to make sure i am not harming the infected area by smoking?

smoking is not good for oral tissue.

reply:
Smoking is not good for oral tissue, so it's best to cut back as much as you can, especially while you're dealing with this.

Regarding your tooth pain: if the pain only happens when you're eating and there's a visible cavity, that tooth will need to be filled. However, if the pain is continuous and the cavity is deep, you may need a root canal treatment — your dentist will be able to determine which applies to you.

In the meantime, for pain relief, start on antibiotics and painkillers, and massage Metrogyl-DG gel over the gum around the affected tooth. Also use Hexidine mouthwash twice a day, after meals.

See your dentist as soon as you can so they can properly assess what's needed.

reply:

patientMessage: Hi doctor, I'm having frequent hair loss and my hair has lost its color and started thinning since 2 years, moreover I'm having diabetes and I masturbate daily. Do the above mentioned problem persists because of diabetes or masturbation. Can it be cured. Will my hair regain its natural health and strength?
doctorNotes:
You seem to have androgenetic alopecia, also called male pattern baldness.
Diabetes does not influence hair loss, but keep it controlled.
Masturbation does not affect hair, but it should be done in moderation.
Consult a dermatologist for a firm diagnosis.
Management suggestions: Continue finasteride 1 mg daily in the morning as you are taking, take biotin 10 mg daily at night and vitamin E 400 mg capsule, apply minoxidil 10% solution twice a day, and cleanse the scalp with ketoconazole shampoo.
Continue treatment for a few months to a few years.
reply:
Thanks for reaching out and sharing your concerns so openly.

Based on what you've described, this sounds like androgenetic alopecia — commonly known as male pattern baldness. To give you a firm diagnosis, I'd recommend seeing a dermatologist.

Regarding your questions: diabetes does not directly cause hair loss, though it's still important to keep your blood sugar well controlled. Masturbation also has no effect on hair health, though it's best done in moderation.

For managing the hair loss, here is what I'd suggest:

- Continue taking **finasteride 1 mg** every morning as you already are
- Take **biotin 10 mg** daily at night
- Take **vitamin E 400 mg** capsule daily
- Apply **minoxidil 10% solution** to the scalp twice a day
- Wash your scalp with **ketoconazole shampoo** regularly

patientMessage: Hi, I have been diagnosed with asthmatic bronchitis, never have had asthma, dont smoke, still having asthma attacks after having bronchitis for a week. Have been having back pains on the right side, below my shoulder blade, had xrays but it seemed normal. I still get those pains when I grasp for air. What is causing the pain.
doctorNotes:
Bronchitis is allergy-related and may develop into asthma over time.
Excessive breathing difficulties tense the respiratory muscles and then cause pain.
Use anti-allergic tablets, bronchodilator spray, analgesics as needed, local painkiller gel, and antacids.
Will refer to an allergy specialist for tests, who may prescribe complete treatment with sublingual immunotherapy for the identified allergens.
reply:
Good that you wrote in with these questions — let me go through what's behind what you're experiencing.

Your bronchitis is allergy-related, and this type of condition can develop into asthma over time. That explains why you're having breathing episodes even though you've never had asthma before.

The back pain you're feeling below your right shoulder blade is connected to your breathing difficulties. When you're struggling to breathe, your respiratory muscles work much harder than usual, and that strain causes them to tense up and become painful — so the pain you feel when gasping for air is coming from those overworked muscles, not from anything sinister in your back, which is reassuring given your X-rays were normal.

For managing this, I'd like you to use anti-allergic tablets, your bronchodilator spray, and analgesics as needed. For the localised back pain, a topical painkiller gel can help, and I'd also like you to take antacids.

I'm going to refer you to an allergy specialist who will run tests to identify your specific allergens. Based on those results, they may recommend a course of sublingual immunotherapy — a treatment aimed at addressing the underlying cause of your allergies rather than just the symptoms.

Let me know if things aren't improving in the meantime.
